title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation scam in which AI-generated content was used to fabricate a plausible news article, complete with named real journalists and public officials, to promote an unlicensed investment platform. The failure is not a malfunction of a deployed AI product but a deliberate misuse of AI generation tools to produce disinformation at scale. The fabricated article sits inside a broader infrastructure of fake websites, fake news articles, and fake advertisements, meaning the deception operates across multiple surfaces simultaneously, making any single point of detection insufficient.

The difficulty of catching this kind of fraud lies in its production economics. AI tools lower the cost of generating credible-looking text and, by implication, credible-looking media environments, so the volume of fraudulent material can grow faster than manual review processes can handle. ASIC's figure of 19,400 scam removals in a single year, representing a 182 percent increase, reflects that dynamic directly. Detection requires either platform-level filtering before publication or consumer-side verification against official registers, neither of which is automatic.

What is not established is that any specific AI company or product was identified as the source of the generation tools used, that Boulder Sparhaven has been the subject of a legal finding rather than a regulatory warning, or that the individuals impersonated suffered any quantified harm beyond reputational association with fraudulent content.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article described a heated interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock that never actually occurred. The fabricated piece promoted Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform that Australian authorities warn against. This incident represents a growing trend of AI-generated investment scams that are becoming increasingly sophisticated and harder to detect.

Australian Securities and Investments Commission data reveals a significant surge in these fraudulent schemes, with the regulator removing 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase. The scammers frequently impersonate well-known Australians including Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Alan Kohler, businessman Dick Smith, and mining magnate Gina Rinehart. Rather than using isolated fake images, criminals now create elaborate webs of deception involving fake websites, news articles, and advertisements. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing and to be skeptical of endorsements from famous figures.
